Add aggressive low-pass filter to the Daisy Seed base board output  This is from me looking at the HF noise from the Daisy Seed on the oscilloscope, and then checking what the Hothouse padal looks like.  The Hothouse actually looks really clean - kudos to Ricky Sheaves.  The reason seems to be a rather aggressive low-pass filter with the 3dB point at 22kHz.  That will attenuate some of the audio band too, but looks like it's the right thing to do considering the noise.  (Of course, the Hothouse also does an op-amp to buffer the end result. My silly discrete component board does not.  That will affect the end result too, but the output impedance should already be pretty low for a guitar pedal even without the extra output buffer).  Change the sim to have a simulated 100 Ohm impedance signal output from the Daisy Seed so that the AC simulation makes sense.  Without that this just resulted in nonsensical output filtering.  While looking at the AC response, also change the input caps to 4.7uF - I think that's what I used for the test board, and you definitely want something bigger than 0.47uF for bass response.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add very incomplete and broken stm32 board  The potential plan is to maybe try to actually recreate a subset of what the Daisy Seed does, and have it populated at jlcpcb.  Because I'm not excited about hand-soldering the kinds of components this will need (although so far I've picked stuff that should be doable, so maybe I change my mind and just go for a stencil).  This is probably all kinds of broken garbage.  And it's very incomplete. I've done a MCU board before, but that was years ago.  I've never done one of the stm32 ones.  Not yet done: SWD, proper USB, and the PCM3060.  And whatever else I'm missing and haven't even thought of yet.  Also, since I've picked a stm32 part that I could maybe solder at home, it's one that doesn't have enough pins brought out for SDRAM.  So I'd be limited to the internal 1MB of RAM.  Put another way: don't for a moment think that this replaces a real Daisy Seed.  That board works, was designed by somebody who knew what they were doing, and is clearly superior.  In contrast, this is me doing silly things again, in the name of trying to learn something new.  In other and more uplifting news: the dual-JFET LS844 input circuit on the base board actually does work, and seems to work very well indeed.  I've only built one board, but that one looked very linear and clean on a triangle wave all the way between 10mVp-p to 4Vp-p in the whole 20Hz-20kHz band.  In fact I checked it from 10Hz all the way up to 1Mhz.  And yes, it was recognizably a signal even at 1MHz.  Admittedly at that point it looked much more like a sine-wave and had attenuated quite a lot.  There's an intentional RF filter in the input path, so that's basically expected.  In fact that signal looked *so* good that I'm suspicious that I did something wrong.  But at 4Vp-p I followed the input and the output on the oscillosope all the way from 20Hz to 20kHz, and they looked visually indistinguishable and the signals were on top of each other from 70Hz up (20-70Hz you'd see the triangle wave bowing a bit due to AC coupling).  At 10mVp-p, you could definitely see noise, but I'm not sure how much of it comes from the actual circuits, and how much of it is from cables (ie comparing a nice direct BNC cable from the signal generator to the oscilloscope with one that goes through two guitar patch cables and the 1/4" jacks: not exactly equivalent signal integrity).  The HF noise is maybe 2mVp-p (looks like ~1mV if I limit the scope bandwidth to 20MHz), so it's a noticeable fraction of the 10mV signal, but on the whole this still looks like my best input path by far.  The 10mVp-p signal still looks good at 100kHz (and also still recognizably a signal at 1MHz).  NOTE! That's just the input signal path when jumpered directly to the output.  When adding the Daisy Seed on the test board into the path it is a different thing entirely, of course.  *That* noise looks more like 100mVp-p, and I have to look at a 1Vp-p signal to make it really recognizable.  The Daisy Seed still *sounds* pretty good, because the noise seems to be mainly HF noise at 450kHz or something - I suspect it ends up being the 3.3V switching power supply on the Daisy Seed that presumably changes frequency based on load.  It just looks horrible on the oscilloscope, but sounds way better than any of my analog effects did.  Also, looking at the waveform, the Daisy Seed delay - without any effect active - is about 5.2ms.  That's with the Hothouse "ShimmerVerb" effect loaded, it might depend on some setup.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Regardless, this really confused me when generating some rather invalid gerbers. It's hopefully right now.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Try attaching the Daisy Seed directly on the base board  Ok, so to fit this thing, I needed to play some games, and also get rid of the third potentiometer.  So now it only has two pots, and the Daisy Seed needs to be the unsoldered kind, where you solder low-profile pin headers to the "wrong" side of the board.  IOW, the Daisy Seed gets mounted upside down on the top of the base board, and then it kind of fits.  I say "kind of", because this is all without a stomp switch.  I haven't decided on what I want to do about that.  The switch connector is just holes for a pin header - or more likely, two wires.  I do think I should just give up on the 1950A form factor, which would make all these games a complete non-issue.  But it's not like the whole thing makes any sense to begin with, so why start being sensible now?  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add input signal re-biasing to the Daisy Seed after all  Yes, the Daisy Seed ends up AC-coupling the input, and will re-bias it to the mid-point of the analog voltage range for the audio codec.  But thinking some more about it, I started worrying about the capacitor used. In particular, it might very well be a low-voltage one, and the dual JFET input will have a buffered output voltage in the 5V+ range.  Simulation puts the signal level centered at 7.4V, but who knows what an actual LS844 will be.  For all I know the dual JFET thing really would want more of a voltage range than a 9V positive supply and it will not work very well in real life, but we'll see.  [ I can always go back to the single MMBF5103 as an input buffer, that   worked fine and is more than sufficient for a guitar pedal -   particularly one of my design.    The whole "let's used two matched JFET's" is really me being rather   silly, after having seen reports of it having particularly good THD by   Rod Elliott (ESP) [1] and Erno Borbely [2].    ESP uses the matched JFET as a current source, Erno Borbely as a   current sink. Mostly it shouldn't make any difference, but I randomly   did the current sink thing. And that does end up with the signal at a   higher voltage ]  Regardless, it's entirely possible that the AC coupling on the Daisy Seed uses a capacitor that is rated for something like 6.3V, which is common for smaller SMT caps.  That would make sense, since the assumption is an incoming signal around ground, with the center of the analog voltage at 1.6V.  So my assumption that the AC coupling of the Daisy Seed would make it unnecessary to do any AC coupling on the base board signal was clearly horribly flawed.  Let's fix it.  I wonder what the next horribly flawed idea is?  Link: https://sound-au.com/articles/jfet-design.htm#s5 [1] Link: https://pearl-hifi.com/06_Lit_Archive/14_Books_Tech_Papers/Borbely_Erno/JFETS_The_New_Frontier.pdf [2] Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Finish down-converting a couple of the old boards to KiCad 9.0  This just does the "load into kicad, fix up, save" dance for the plain base board.  Also do the Octaver and compressor effects boards to check.  This finishes the conversion back to KiCad 9.0.  I think I'll just leave the other boards alone: I think I'm done with them anyway, and we'll just leave them in that zombie state for posterity.  I just wanted to check that the scripted conversion seems to mostly work for these things.  You do want to do some manual fixups for this stage: removing the use of real sound files from simulation (since it doesn't exist in released kicad/ngspice versions), updating symbols and footprints from the libraries, things like that.  Then refill the PCBs and run all the checks to make sure it all seems sane.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Scripted down-conversion of the rest of the files to kicad 9.0 format  This just does the minimal conversion to make kicad-9 almost happy with the down-conversion.  It was done with this very hacky script:    files=$(git grep -l '"9.99"')   sed -i 's/(version [0-9]*)/(version 20231212)/' $files   sed -i 's/(generator_version "9.99")/(generator_version "9.0")/' $files   sed -i 's/(power global)/(power)/' $files   sed -i '/(capping [a-z]*)/ d' $files   sed -i '/(filling [a-z]*)/ d' $files   sed -i '/duplicate_p[ia][nd]_numbers_are_jumpers/ d' $files   perl -0777 -i -pe 's/\t*\(((tenting)|(covering)|(plugging))\s*\(front\s*\w*\)\s*\(back\s*\w*\)\s*\)\s//gs' $files  please don't use that on anything you care about without checking things extensively (and not on any repo with whitespace or other special characters in filenames, there's no quoting or anything: this was very much ad-hoc hacky stuff).  Note: this only makes kicad-9 able to load the files, so that they can then be properly converted by saving them from kicad 9 after doing some cleanups (synchronizing symbols, refilling pcb, yadda yadda).  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Downgrade Daisy Seed boards to kicad v9.0  Since I don't do audio signal simulation with the Daisy Seed boards, let's try to downcovert to the standard kicad version to make it easier to use without having to have a self-compiled version.  Kicad doesn't make this particularly easy, I'm afraid.  Let's hope this didn't do anything bad.  It still simulates, and looks superficially ok.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Create a pedal design based on the Electrosmith Daisy Seed platform  This tries to make the pedal actually useful by making the audio side use the Daisy Seed from Electrosmith [1]  I've had the board for the last six months, but up until now didn't feel ready to use it.  I even built the Hothouse pedal kit around it, and exchanged some emails with both Andrew Ikenberry (Electrosmith) and Ricky Sheaves (of Hothouse pedal from Cleveland Music Co), but never even flashed it up to test.  But now that I'm getting bored with trying variations of the basic analog base board, let's switch things up a bit and do a base board for the Daisy Seed instead.  Because assuming I don't mess anything up, it's obviously going to sound much better and be a lot more flexible than some silly analog distortion circuit from half a century ago.  [ This is just a worse version of the Hothouse pedal, using a crazy dual   JFET thing for input buffering just because the sane thing that the   Hothouse does - using a much cheaper and more capable op-amp - feels a   bit boring.    So unlike the Hothouse, this is a mono board and objectively less   useful. Go get the real thing from [2]. This is just another board in   the endless series called "Linus is trying new ways to do pointless   things" ]  So this takes my traditional base board, turns it around so that the power and audio connectors go on the bottom of the board, and puts the control pots on the top side.  That way all the mechanical hardware is on the base board.  I think this is what I probably should have done originally, but it forces a fixed layout for pots and switches, which didn't appeal to me in the original design, because the pot connections depend on the effect.  However, since the enclosures are such a pain, a fixed layout is actually probably a good thing, and with the Electrosmith Daisy Seed, the pots are all connected the same way - as resistor diviers to ADC inputs.  And since this puts all the mechanicals on that base, the effect board now has a lot more space.  Which wasn't an issue with the original trivial effects, but now that I'm trying to fit the whole Daisy Seed on that thing, it suddenly becomes a major issue.  Will it fit? Naah - the Daisy Seed board is just too high in the Z dimension. But I'm thinking about it. There's a distant plan.  This also updates the 1590A footprint for the new fixed 3-pot layout and for the new board connector placement. And incidentally also fixes the location for the LED and the switch that had been moved in a long time ago.  The effects board then pretty much just connects the pin headers from the connector board to the Daisy Seed. There's a capacitor in there too, but that's literally it.  This does it all with a custom Daisy Seed symbol and footprint.  There were already versions of that in the KiCad libraries, but I'm not a fan. The standard KiCad version has the whole Daisy seed as a keep-out area, and I want to be able to put low-profile things under the board without DRC complaints.  My custom one also ends up just using the Hothouse pin names (so "POT1" for the first potentiometer, rather than GPIO16/ADC1). So it's a bit clearer what is going on by being specific to my particular use.  Link: https://electro-smith.com/ [1] Link: https://clevelandmusicco.com/hothouse-diy-digital-signal-processing-platform-kit/ [2] Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Try LDO for positive voltage rail cleaning  As mentioned, I don't think I'll actually build this, because it seems pointlessly complicated.  But I did the basic design and layout for it just in case.  I think I'll go back to the single-rail design and keep the MOSFET switching.  I also think I need to come up with a new project.  I'm kind of running out of ideas of small projects to do that I can build and test.  I like the switching circuit, but I'm losing interest in the effects board side since I still can't actually play guitar.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add AP2202-ADJ LDO symbol to my parts library  I don't think I'll actually end up using this, because the negative voltage generation just ends up being more pain than it is worth, but I think I'll do one last test-run of things with a nice linear voltage regulator to make that positive rail more solid.  I've been here before: I'd like to have a dual rail voltage for so many reasons, but the end result is just rather noisy.  Not just on the actual negative rail, but on the incoming positive rail too.  The dual inductor thing does seem less noisy than most, but it still requires just more work.  Even the traditional charge pump wasn't great.  It's all fixable, but the fixes tend to end up making things more complicated than simply rebiasing the signal to the middle of the positive rail.  This is made much worse by the whole "modular base and effects board" approach I have taken: it means that the base board then always ends up being overly complicated, when the effect board may not need a negative rail at all, or may not need very much power at all.  In fact, it might not need the signal being re-bias back to ground because in many cases the effects board will rebias the signal anyway.  So this is all self-inflicted pain.  But I'll continue doing this simply because I'm trying things out, and certainly learning things in the process.  I do note that my plain base board is very simple and works really quite well, but does rely on clean power input.  So it wants a good low-noise guitar pedal power supply.  Which is admittedly not that hard to find, and kind of expected for most guitar pedals.  I then mess things up with my own power supply games.  But here we are: add a LDO to allow cleaning up the mess that generating that negative rail results in.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Update the buffered base board  The JFET switching worked fine, but since this all started as an exercise in using MOSFETs, let's just go all in on that, and use the MOSFETs for switching the signal too.  Due to the body diode, you need two MOSFETs in series for the signal switching, so it's four MOSFETs instead of two JFETs, but despite that the end result is actually simpler.  And those dual MOSFET things are common and dirt cheap, unlike the special matched JFET package.  Since I can just continue to use the dual complementary MOSFETs, I can use PMOS for one signal and NMOS for the other, and share all the gate circuit.  Plus no need for a diode to protect the gate current messing with the signal.  Also update the resistor value in the switching circuit and make the time constant be 100ms.  That seems to make it more reliable in testing, although I'm not convinced my testing with the original value was all that great.  The soft-switch circuit does seem to work, though.  Also, since the LED pin on the board connectors has never been used, let's just re-purpose that as a negative voltage pin for the effect board.  If some effect board wants to touch the LED status, it might as well just connect to the LED itself.  Having access to a dual voltage rail would seem to be a lot more important.  Finally - and probably most importantly for actual sound and current effects boards - add a low-pass filter on the voltage lines.  Because as expected, the negative power supply did add a lot of noise to the VIN line.  The base board itself doesn't actually care, but the effects boards do.  An actual LDO would be better, but I don't have any simple fixed ones in my parts library (except for the 5V one, which seems a bit sad). Current effects boards don't use a lot of current and only care about the voltage being stable, so let's try this simple model.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Buffered base: use negative rail for JFET switching  This _still_ doesn't do any actual buffering, but with the negative rail, we now no longer need to rebase the signals to some mid-point voltage, and we can just leave the signals ground-references and use the negative rail for switching.  That streamlines the signal path, and will make it easier to just insert an opamp or two in there too.  But I remain more interested in getting the switching side sorted out properly, so that's the primary goal here.  This tweaks the push-on push-off circuit a bit too, since taht one now needs to switch between positive and negative voltages rather than VIN and ground.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add negative power rail to the buffered base design  The negative voltage isn't actually _used_ anywhere yet, but this is prep-work for making that buffered base board do the long promised buffering, as I'm currently leaning towards opamps.  The LT3462A is very easy to use, but in a probably completely misguided attempt at keeping any stray ground return currents on the power supply side, I added a ground plane keepout.  No isolation, but an attempt to at least make the easy path for any return currents to stay in that "power supply area" and hopefully not show up around the analog parts.  Somebody who knows what they are about would probably tell me I'm just making things worse.  But I'm a sw engineer, so pretty much by definition I don't know anybody who knows what they are doing.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add LT3462A symbol  I'm going to experiment with a negative power rail one more time, and in the LT3462A I found a DC/DC converter that looks a lot more pleasant than the ones I've tried before.  Not only is it a nice TSOT-23-6 footprint, but it has an integrated schottky diode so it's easy to use.  And it's a fixed frequency dual inductor inverter design, so it should be reasonably quiet in the audio frequency.  I'm not planning to bother with LDOs to clean up the power rails, because the reason for the power rail would be the op-amp for buffering, and the PSRR of any quality opamp should make it all irrelevant.  I dunno.  Every time I've tried this, it's just been noise hell, so this is probably a bad idea.  Even when you can't actually _hear_ the noise, it ends up just messing with the signal on the scope and making it harder to judge whether the circuit is doing well or not.  But I keep trying.  What was the definition of insanity again? I forget.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Split the buffered base over multiple schematic pages, do PCB layout  So this thing is still mis-named, in that it doesn't actually buffer the signal at all, it only does the transistor soft-switching.  But I _will_ add buffering at some point, it's just not the interesting part of this all, since I've done that part before.  But because I wrote explanations for the push-on / push-off circuit, and because I split things up into small parts, the schematic was getting pretty crowded.  So I decided to split up the actually interesting part of the schematic - the switching side - onto a schematic page of its own.  And while doing that, I moved the simulation infrastructure to its own page too.  That leaves the toplevel page pretty empty with mainly just the connectors and the basic signal and power filtering, but that's where the buffers will go eventually.  And because it simulates fine, I want to actually see if it works in reality.  So this also does the PCB layout.  There's tons of room left for any future buffering circuit, whether I then do it with discrete JFETs or decide that op-amps are the sane thing here.  I used a random regular tactile switch - which I don't actually have in my parts library.  I'll just wire up two wires and test it that way (and I do have some momentary SPDT stomp switches around that I can attach to the wires).  But longer-term, one of the points of this kind of electronic switching is that you can do it multiple ways, and aren't limited to a physical switch - or indeed just a single one.  So maybe I'll do some remote switching thing, or play around with using a hall effect sensor and a magnet, or whatever.  There are always new things to learn about...  But let's make sure the basics of this thing actually works first.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Buffered base: add RF filter after JFET switches  It turns out that getting rid of the switching pop seems to be as simple as that.  Maybe time to do PCB layout and see if reality matches simulation?  I do think I should do the buffer that this doesn't do despite the name. That was the intent, but then it worked so well without it..  An op-amp would be the sane thing to do, but since I've been on a "discrete components" tear, I suspect I'd just do a JFET voltage follower.  But then I feel like I should make up for the inevitable signal loss. Or use a common source thing that does a phase reversal? That seems wrong too.  Perhaps do another dual JFET for a common source both at input and output?  Decisions, decisions.  Anyway, this doesn't do any of that.  This just gets rid of the switching pop in simulation.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Wire the soft-switch up to actually switch signal and LED  Surprisingly, this actually seems to work fine.  In simulation only, of course.  And not surprisingly, according to the same simulation, it has an impressively horrible pop at switching time.  This very much reminds me of the broken "Tremolo doubling as a metronome" thing, which was due to the exact same thing: very harsh and sudden driving of the JFET gate.  It's made worse by the MOSFET switching having the same thing.  Big voltage spike when turning off, presumably due to capacitive parasitics or whatever.  Possibly helped by adding a resistor at the gate or something, but unlike the tremolo, the switching event is rare.  So right now I simply don't care.  I'm just _simulating_ switching things at a 5Hz rate, so it shows up like a sore thumb.  I haven't done layout, and I haven't added a real switch yet, so this is all just simulation.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add the beginnings of a dubious buffered base board  As part of looking at what I should try to use my MOSFETs for, I decided I should finally look at a soft-switch buffered base board.  This is not it, but it starts with a very dubious push-on push-off MOSFET circuit.  I doubt it really works, even if it simulates beautifully.  But I don't simulate any debounce issues etc, although I don't see why it wouldn't deal with that too.  All the real push-on push-off circuits I've seen are more complex than this, which is the main reason why I doubt that my simple circuit really works.  It's a bit *too* simple.  Everybody uses some flip-flop and/or schmitt trigger or other fancier things.  But hey, maybe my google-fu is weak and I just didn't find the right thing and there are even simpler ways to do this.  Plus I admittedly came at this from an odd direction of "what can I do with discrete MOSFETs".  Sane people don't do that.  Anyway, the basic of the push-on push-off circuit is - as always - a capacitor that alternates between being discharged and charged up.  Then two transistors that reinforce each other's state.  In this case, the capacitor is connected to the gate of the PMOSFET through the momentary switch.  So if you press the switch and the capacitor was discharged, the PMOSFET starts conducting, while if you press the switch and the capacitor was charged, the PMOSFET turns off.  The rest of the circuit is just the complementary NMOSFET that then follows the PMOSFET state and re-inforces whatever state it was in, and the resistors to make it all work sanely.  The only important thing is to make sure the resistors have sane values to not do bad things while the switch is pressed.  It all simulates ok, and I don't see why it wouldn't work.  Anyway, this *only* does that silly push-on push-off logic.  It isn't actually hooked up any way yet.  Not even the LED to show the state, much less any JFETs to switch the actual signal around.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add a few dual MOSFET symbols  So I think I mostly understand JFETs, and I did BJT's earlier, so now it's time for some MOSFET love.  Sure, I've used a P-channel MOSFET for the high-side power thing, but that's still just trivial switching.  I need to learn the whole small-signal AC thing and biasing etc.  And since I like the dual transistor form factors, and TSOT-23-6 is about the right size for me, here's three different ones:   - DMN3060LVT: dual N-channel MOSFET  - DMP3164LVT: dual P-channel MOSFET  - DMC3071LVT: dual complementary MOSFET  all three are fairly similar: 30V breakdown voltages, capable of a couple of amps.  The complementary one is a bit beefier and has slightly higher V_{TH} values, but we're still looking at roughly the same kind of thing.  Let's see what I can do with these.  I didn't actually pick these based on any sane and deep characteristics, they may be entirely the wrong thing, but that's what we're going to find out.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Update compressor PCB layout too  This does the new trial matches JFET thing as a board layout too.  I'm really not convinced this was worth it, and the routing and layout are a bit of a mess, but it's all part of the whole learnign experience, and I do want to see if the self-biasing thing actually works in real life or it just happens to look ok in simulation with the particular simulation values.  .. and the usual noise from KiCad inexplicably changing randon things when looking at files.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Compressor: base the compressor level voltage on matched JFET  This is an attempt at basing the compression level voltage on the matched JFET, making the level knob hopefully more reliably sane in the face of different JFET characteristics.  I'm not entirely convinced I shouldn't just use a trim pot, but I do think this is a more interesting approach.  It basically picks the base voltage from the self-biasing voltage of the matched JFET, guaranteeing that the level voltage pot starts close to V_{GSOFF}.  The level pot is then basically controlling the DC bias on top of that.  This also tries to make the actual attentuation circuit clearer and hopefully better.  Both the JFET drain and source are biased to the compression level voltage, while the base is biased to the signal peak detector (the somewhat mis-named "RECT" net).  The source then also gets the signal, and when V_{GS} gets close to zero (ie RECT gets close to LEVEL) the JFET starts conducting and the AC signal is attenuated through the JFET to the capacitor to ground at the drain.  The base gets half the AC signal (on top of the DC peak bias) as before to minimize distortion (ie the AC signal at the base is halfway between the AC signal at source and the lack of AC signal at drain).  This all seems to still simulate well, and the behavior of the level pot seems to mostly make sense.  How well it works with actual random JFET characteristics and whether the matching model works, I don't know.  I still need to actually lay out the PCB, but I think the schematic is getting closer.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Update compressor for the LS844 dual JFET  This is just a quick conversion, not using the matching, just using the LS844 as two independent JFETs.  Because I_{DSS} is lower, the source resistor on the input buffer is bigger, so that if I_{DSS} is just 1.5mA the voltage drop over the resistor can go up to 3.5V.  Similarly, tweak the limit resistor values to give a bigger limit voltage range for the bigger V_{GSOFF} range of the LS844, and make the negative feedback resistor divider bigger to account for higher R_{DSON} of the LS844.  Also remove the partial bypassing of the amplification emitter resistor, since the high-frequency damping of the plain base is no more.  Although maybe it wants a brighter sound?  This seems to simulate ok, although the compression is certainly not identical to the version with the MMBF5103.  That may be real, or may be just different spice model default values and swamped by JFET variations.  Anyway, I'll eventually try the "use self-biasing using the matching JFETs to do automatic levels" eventually, but first I wanted to do the minimal conversion and verify that at least the LS844 model seems to be ok before doing any bigger surgery.  NOTE! This doesn't update the PCB layout for the changes.  Just doing the schematic and simulation checks.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Update the plain base to have a 1k RF resistor  That's what the text on the silkscreen said, but I had tested with a 10k resistor (for a 72kHz low pass filter). convert: add somewhat realtime control interface  This is pretty raw and stupid, but I wanted to try changing the conversion parameters on the fly with a "control file descriptor".  This is currently very limited, and doesn't have an interface for switching the effect itself at runtime (like I do on the hardware: long-press the foot-switch for one second), but at least allows for sending "pot commands" to change the pot values dynamically.  The format is a five-byte ASCII packet of 'pXYY\n', which sets put X to value YY (X being in the range '0'..'3', and YY being '00'..'99').  Why that format? Because right now the only testing I've done is from the terminal, doing something like this:      $ ./convert --control=0 phaser input.raw |                 aplay -c1 -r 48000 -f s32 -B 100  and then you can just type in those commands at the terminal by hand: the "--control=0" is the magic that says that fd 0 is a control channel.  Very combersome, very stupid, but hey, it works.  Note that I'm back to using 'aplay' for this, because with ffplay the latency is absolutely horrible.  Something like three seconds of audio later does any pot command take effect, because ffplay has slurped in a lot of data into its input buffers.  In contrast, with 'aplay', the effect is basically instantaneous, particularly with that "-B 100" that keeps the buffering to a very reasonable 100ms.  If there is a flag for ffplay that makes it not buffer input very much, I haven't found it (and yes, I tried the obvious ones, but no, I didn't do any exhaustive search since aplay works fine for me).  It should be very possible to wrap a UI around this, and I should also add some command to switch the effect at runtime too.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Clean up integer type system a bit, and prep for extensions  I had started out using 'uint' because that came from the pico sdk and seemed to be common there, but it's a horrible type that doesn't really specify the size and is just a lazy form of the standard types.  And for historical reasons I despise 'uint32_t' and friends: it may be universal now, but it used to be one of those things where system headers didn't reliably have them, so you ended up with #ifdef's to do your own versions anyway, and it was all just unnecessarily painful.  So I'm ornery, but I'm used to the kernel types that are nice and short and simple: 'u32' and friends.  Let's just use them.  And because the target hardware (RP2354A with dual Cortex-M33 cores) should have a fast 32x32->64 integer multiply with accumulate, I'm considering doing some fixed-point ops in paths where the 32-bit floats aren't necessary, and would avoid the type conversion overheads.  So I'm adding the s64/u64 types too in preparation for that.  It's possible that I should just do all of the LFO as 32-bit fractional integers (it already largely is).  Maybe even use fixed-point for the biquad code, which is what the TAC5112 does internally.  That would give higher precision than using floats thanks to a bigger mantissa, but with the caveat that the range would be very limited and would require a lot of care.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix final float -> int conversion overflow  The final conversion from float to s32 does  	sample = (int)(out * 0x80000000);  and that overflows for 1.0, turning it into the most negative integer number.  I could just make the thing multiply by 0x7ffffffff instead, and miss out on turning -1 to that most negative number, but I think the best model is to just explicitly check for overflow by testing the sign of the float vs the resulting integer.  That deals with any small overflow outside the [-1,1] range too, which allows the effects to be a bit lazy if they want to (although gross overflow could then result in the sign overflowing "twice" and not be caught, so effects shouldn't be *too* lazy).  This may explain some crackling in anything that ended up doing the full FP range (although you really should try to avoid that anyway).  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix 'discont' effect potentiometer behavior  I messed up when I imported the discont effect from the RP2354A code: I had gone back-and-forth in that repo on just how much you could change the pitch, alternating between "arbitrary", "by semitones" and "fixed to fourths, fifths and octaves".  When I then moved the code over to this simulation repo, I decided to go back to "arbitrary", and that people could just make the pot value negative, so that you could just go down an octave by doing      ./discont -1 ....  That was technically true, but it means that now if I want to test things on the RP2354A hardware after being happy with it in simulation, I'll always have to mess with this potentiometer mapping.  So go back to the assumption that the pot values should primarily be floating point values in the range [0,1], and that 0 means "one octave down" and 1 means "one octave up" (approximately, because we're using that quick-and-dirty very inexact fastpow2_m1() function).  So now it takes the pot value, and multiplies it by two and subtracts one to get the "power of two". Thus turning [0,1] into [-1,1].  In simulations, you can still use negative values if you want, so that (if we had a better 'pow2()' approximation) you could do      ./discont -0.5 ...  to go down two octaves, or use '2' to go up three octaves).  The actual pitch shifting does actually work for those kinds of ranges, but fastpow2_m1() does not, so currently a pot value outside 0..1 gives pretty nonsensical actual step values.  Replace 'fastpow2_m1(x)' with 'pow(2.0,x)-1' if you want to play silly games with a silly effect.  [ And again, just to clarify: the "pitch shifting" of the discont.h   effect is really not anything like a real pitch shift. It's walking   the delay line at non-unity speeds to speed up or slow down the   signal, and then abruptly jumping back or forward to catch up to real   time.    It then tries to hide those discontinuities from the jumping around by   using two different delays and mixing them together with the   discontinuity points faded away, which is why the effect is called   "discont" ]  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Fix math library linking causing link errors for 'gensin'  The Makefile used LDFLAGS to set "-lm" to link in the math library for the 'sin()' function use in gensin.c.  That is wrong, and causes the '-lm' to be too early in the implicit executable rule, resulting in potentially undefined references at link time.  It just happened to work for me even with the wrong placement of the linker flag.  The reason is simply that my build environment used dynamic linking for the math library, which brings in all of libm.so regardless of what functions you use.  A static link that only brings in the actually used functions would then not have seen the use of 'sin()' (yet) and then the wrong placement causes      gensin.c: undefined reference to `sin'  Fix it by using the proper Makefile variable for the math library: LDLIBS.  Reported-by: Max McEvoy <maxmcevoy@gmail.com> Reported-by: Thomas <thomas.blakely@gmx.com> Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Cache 24c02 eeprom contents, write to it more carefully  The 24c02 eeprom isn't the fanciest of chips, and when it is busy writing it falls off the i2c bus - and the write can take up to 5ms.  That really wasn't an issue when we only wrote back the effect state when switching effects manually.  The writes were naturally limited by the UI update speed.  But the new WebMIDI interface with the "save all effects" option means that suddenly writes weren't limited by the UI update speed at all, and they started failing.  The most straightforward solution to this is to just cache the whole (little) eeprom state in RAM, and have a "eeprom_task()" that writes back dirty data with the required 5ms delays.  In fact, to keep things simple, we'll just keep it to the same UI update limit it used to have.  So now loading the effect just reads it from the RAM cache, and saving the effect just writes it back to the RAM cache and marks it dirty for later writeback.  In fact, since we buffer it anyway, let's just make the writes be limited to 8 bytes at a time, so that if I were to ever make the mistake of getting an older version of the 24c02, it will still work.  The chips I have all have a 16-byte page size, but some old versions apparently have 8-byte pages and writing 16 bytes at a time wouldn't work (the second half would just overwrite the first half).  Reading the 24c02 doesn't have any of those issues, and you can just slurp in the whole 256-byte thing in one go at boot time.  This seems to fix all the saving problems that the new WebMIDI code exposed.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Convert effects to metadata-driven boiler plate generation  This is the actual effect format update mentioned in the previous commit: express the boiler plate details in the comment at the top of the effect so that it can be auto-generated.  Part of that is that now the default values can be much more sanely expressed: instead of setting the defaults as the particular integer values the pot takes, express them in the user-visible units.  So the default noise gate level value can now be described as      // POT: "Level" LINEAR(-100.0 -40.0) = -70.0 dB  instead of the inscrutable      EFFECT_POT("Level", desc_dB, gate_pot0_level, 0),   // -70dB  where the default value of 0 ended up indeed being -70dB, but we had to have a comment to that effect because it was so non-obvious (it came from the fact that gate_pot0_level() did a linear interpolation between -100 and -40, and -70 is the middle value).  So now the pot values make a lot more sense and defaults are easier to see and set.  This also means that instead of having the pot values be -60 to +60 (in order to make the default "noon" be zero and needing no initializer), since we auto-generate the defaults we can make the actual internal values be the more straightforward 0..120 range - not only matching what we did for MIDI, but also simplifying a lot of the helper math cases.  As a result, the pot arrays are now done as 'unsigned char'.  While doing all this, I also noticed that the ->describe() function is just entirely historical: it used to depend on the pot value for when the enumerations were done as a separate hack.  But these days enumeration pots are an integral part of the pot description, and the ->describe() functions were all just returning the unit string.  So get rid of the function pointer indirection, and just make it have a simple and straightforward 'const char *unit' string.  This all makes the 'gen_effect' python script a bit bigger, but that is more than made up for by the boiler plate removal in the effects themselves, so not only does it make things clearer, this all removes more lines than it adds.  And equally importantly, it means that now the Web UI actually can convert the raw pot values into sensible units, because it too can take the pot descriptions into account.  Some other minor UI updates while at it.  All the python and JS scripting itself was obviously all done by AI. Some day I might care enough to learn to actually write python, but for now I'm perfectly happy just reading the end result.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Move all effects into 'effects/' subdirectory  .. leaving the audio helper headers in 'audio/'.  I'll make the auto-generation script pick up the effects list automatically from the files in that directory, but I'll do that separately: this is just the minimal file move.  Note that it's not enough to just enumerate the effects: the order of effects also matters, so it's not quite as simple as just generating the effect list from a simple directory listing.  So the next step is to add some more metadata to the effects files.  Right now the only "metadata" is the dummy wrapper macro just to mark the pot descriptions.  I want to extend that too - it would be good to actually contain the description and mapping of values too, so that instead of using C function pointers the pot descriptions would have a higher level abstraction that can be not only turned into the C code, but also used for the Web MIDI side.  And the effect itself should have its own metadata - not just the ordering requirement (as some kind of "priority number"), but the effect name (and shortname) would be exposed too.  I'll have to think about it some more, but my rough plan would be to have the metadata at the top of the effect file in a comment block that is trivially parsed, and instead of having 'gen_effects.py' just generate the trivial     #include "../effects/{base}.h"  thing for effect_map.h, it would generate all the boiler plate for pot values translations and all of 'struct effect' for that effect.  Make all the metadata simple enough that it can be easily translated into both the actual C code running on the microcontroller, but also the JS code running in the web app so that the Web MIDI UI shows proper pot value ranges etc.  The above is a bit handwavy - I'll have to experiment.  But my thinking would be that the gate effect - just to pick a random example - would go from having pot functions and a 'struct effect' like this:      static float gate_pot0_level(signed char pot)     {         // -100dB .. -40dB is 0.01mV..10mV peak signal level         // If your noise floor is anywhere near -100dB, you don't need the         // gate in the first place, but maybe it's a good way to actually         // _see_ what your noise floor is...         return linear_pot(pot, -100.0f, -40.0f);     }     [...]     static struct effect gate_effect = {         .name = "Noise Gate",         .short_name = "GATE",         .init = gate_init,         .step = gate_step,         .pots = {             EFFECT_POT("Level", desc_dB, gate_pot0_level, 0),       // -70dB             EFFECT_POT("Attack", desc_ms, gate_pot1_attack, -42),   // ~1.5ms             EFFECT_POT("Release", desc_ms, gate_pot2_release, -30), // ~150ms         }     };  to having a comment header at the top of the effect:      // NAME: Noise Gate [GATE]     // PRIORITY: 1     //    POT: "Level" LINEAR(-100 -40) dB     //    POT: "Attack" LINEAR(0 10) ms     //    POT: "Release" LINEAR(50 500) ms  and gen_effects.py would just generate the boilerplate code for the interfaces, while the actual real meat of the effect (the init and step functions) would remain as-is.  As always, the EQ effect is special, because it does that whole graph thing.  So we'd have to have a special case for that, but that would probably be just a simple      //    GRAPH: eq_graph  at least for now, and only graphing the frequency response on the pedal, not in the Web UI thing.  Anyway - that's the plan.  But for now, just separate out the effects headers from the other code.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Merge https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal  Merge effect updates from Ricky Sheaves.  This makes some of the effects quite a bit cheaper in memory and/or in CPU use.  It enables flush-to-zero for denormals which can make a big difference, uses a few less filters in the reverb, and makes the echo effect use 16-bit integers for the delay path, saving a lot of memory.  I made the %fpscr register accesses use the compiler built-ins instead of inline asm - it's not like I dislike the inline asm in general, but in this case it seems simpler to just use the compiler infrastructure.  Also, Ricky added an isb instruction to flush the pipeline - that's one of those "technically correct" things to do to synchronize the fpscr access, but it really doesn't matter in this case.  Even if there were FPU instructions in flight (and there aren't), we simply don't care that deeply. So keep it simple and stupid.  * https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal:   Echo: replace float[65536] delay line with int16_t[32768]   Enable hardware FTZ on both cores; drop `reverb_flush()`   Reverb: revert to 8 comb filters and 4 Schroeder allpass filters

Change pot value range from -100..+100 to -60..+60  So "100" looks like a rounder number to a human, and that's obviously why I picked that original range.  But the -100..+100 range does not map very well to MIDI, which sends 7-bit numbers in the 0..127 range.  I started out with -63..+63 originally, but that really doesn't work when some of the settings (like the "octaves" for the pitch shifter) really want nice divisors.  So '60' it is, and in some ways it is actually a "rounder" number than 100, in that it divides nicely into even more cases than 100 does.  While 100 is natural in base-10, it is only divisible by combinations of two and five.  In contrast 60 is divisible by combinations of two, three and five, and so maps well to things like that octave setting.  I don't think the reduced range (201 steps down to "only" 121 steps) is actually noticeable.  We'll see.  There's "high-res MIDI" that sends values in two parts, but that seems overkill.  The slider UI was already limited to only displaying 128 values simply due to the resolution of the display, so ...  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Echo: replace float[65536] delay line with int16_t[32768]  The `float array[65536]` delay line was consuming 256 KB -- 59% of the entire 434 KB bss -- leaving only 7.5 KB of headroom against the 520 KB SRAM limit. With `copy_to_ram` in effect, text + bss share the same pool. A 7.5 KB margin is far too uncomfortable.  `audio/util.h`: - Add `__sample_array_write_s16` / `sample_array_write_s16`: writes a   `[-1, 1]` float to an `int16_t` cell as `val * 32767`. - Add `__sample_array_read_s16` / `sample_array_read_s16`: converts two   adjacent `int16_t` cells to float via `1/32767` and returns the   linearly interpolated result. Same ring-buffer bitmask logic as the   float variants.  `audio/echo.h`: - `echo.array`: `float[65536]` (256 KB) -> `int16_t[32768]` (64 KB).   Saves 192 KB. bss drops from 434 KB to 238 KB; SRAM headroom goes   from 7.5 KB to ~199 KB. (!!!) - `ECHO_DELAY_MAX_S`: 0.800 -> 0.672. The smaller array holds 32768   samples at 48 kHz = 0.683 s. There's still plenty of margin for wow/flutter   modulation. This tighter delay range is still in Maestro EP-1/2 territory. - `ECHO_DELAY_LOG2_RATIO`: 4.0 -> 3.75 to match. - `read_pos` clamp: 65534.0 -> 32766.0 to match the new buffer size. - Read/write calls updated to `sample_array_read_s16` /   `sample_array_write_s16`. - And here's the controversial change:16-bit quantization noise sits at ~-96 dBFS (CD quality), below the guitar noise floor, and is further attenuated by the playback LPF on every pass. We're emulating a tape recorder from the 1960s, which had a dynamic range of ~65-75 dBFS. This roughly maps to an 11 to 13-bit digital scale. So, arguably, it's much more authentic now ;) - Change default pot values:   - `Time`: 46 -> 55 (~374.7 ms via the log taper).   - `WowFlut`: 0 -> -50 (25% depth via `linear_pot`).  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Enable hardware FTZ on both cores; drop `reverb_flush()`  `enable_ftz()` sets the FZ bit (24) in FPSCR via inline assembly on both cores at startup. The Cortex-M33 VFPv5 FPU handles subnormals in hardware rather than via a software trap, but still takes a 5-20x penalty per operation. Any feedback path that decays to sub-1e-38 will hit this without FTZ enabled, not just reverb's comb filters.  The old `reverb_flush()` only protected `filterstore` in the comb loop. Hardware FTZ covers every float op in the chain: allpass buffers, echo feedback, and any future effect, without per-site code needed.  FPSCR is per-core state, so `enable_ftz()` is called in both `main()` and `audio_processing()`.  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>
Reverb: revert to 8 comb filters and 4 Schroeder allpass filters  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Use 'copy_to_ram' in order to avoid running out of flash  Now with a lot more effects, we started to lose samples when enabling the more expensive ones.  And when I did some testing with unrolling loops to improve code quality actually made it worse.  The actual performance issue ends up being that now that we have more effects, we're also blowing out the XIP cache.  It's only 16kB in size, and once you start missing in the XIP cache you get the whole hot of waiting for flash.  Which really hurts on that simple in-order core.  Now, we don't have a ton of SRAM on the rp2354 either, and obviously 'copy_to_ram' will mean that now we have even less, when the boot phase will copy the code into that precious resource.  But we have enough for the current effects, and with this simple one-liner I can enable every single effect without any missing samples.  It's definitely getting to the point where I think any future effects will have to start kicking out some less worthy existing ones.  The pitch shifter is probably bound to be the first to go, even if I enjoy how ridiculous it sounds.  We could try to be more granular, and only move the functions that run as part of the audio loop on the second core into RAM, but I'm not sure it's worth the effort compared to the one-liner build setting.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Merge https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal  Pull new and updated effects from Ricky Sheaves:  "This is fun. I spent hours today converting code from various   projects.    In addition to the effects you already have, these round out the   'essentials' rather nicely, I think. These are 90% of everything   I use on a weekly basis:      Vibrato 	A must for organ-like tones (and full-blown chorus with the MIX at 50%)      Reverb 	This one took some tuning given the CPU budget and the growing FX chain      Preamp 	Tube / JFET saturation (different than Boost)      Tremolo 	Standard issue; I added the somewhat-rare harmonic mode      Echo 	No big changes, but I had to tune it once Reverb + Echo couldn't 	play nicely    The commit messages pretty much cover it all"  Note that the reverb effect in particular is fairly expensive, and it's easy to overwhelm the poor little RP2354 when enabling lots of effects.  The UI will not keep you from overwhelming the MCU, but you'll notice it: the sound turns scratchy and bad, and the right-hand LED will grow more brightly to show signal problems.  [ The right-hand LED also glows brightly for signal clipping, but it's   typically pretty easy to tell whether it glowing due to clipping or   due to a sample loss due to a overwhelmed CPU.    They sound very different - a rather "scratchy" sound when missing   samples vs a loud distorted signal. And their behavior pattern is   different too: the clipping obviously happens with loud signals and   tends to be temporary, while the overwhelmed CPU tends to be a pretty   constant thing depending purely on the number (and type) of effects   enabled, not the amplitude of the output ]  * https://github.com/clevelandmusicco/GuitarPedal:   Tremolo: fix the harmonic tremolo level drop   Add tremolo effect with NORM and HARM modes   Reduce reverb CPU load; minor echo optimisations   Reverb: expand to 12 combs/6 allpasses, add per-comb LFO modulation   Add Freeverb reverb effect (Schroeder-Moorer, mono 48 kHz)   Add preamp and vibrato effects   Tape Echo: remove cruft and tweak performance

eeprom: only use 16 bytes per effect save area  I originally reserved 32 bytes per effect for saving to the eeprom, with the idea that I'd have a secondary save area and only a fairly small number of effects.  Except I never did that secondary save area, and the effects have kept growing.  Since I just picked the simplest 2kbit i2c eeprom there is, the whole save area is just 256 bytes in size.  That makes the i2c programming very simple, but it meant that with 32 bytes per effect it could only save 8 effects.  We already have more than that (counting the USB "effect"), and Ricky has been doing a few more.  So let's just get rid of the theoretical secondary save area, and give each effect just 16 bytes of eeprom.  While doing that, I'm also updating the checksum to cover more of the effect data, so that when you change an effect (rename it, or to add new state or whatever), there's a higher likelihood that the checksum won't match some random old setting, and the state will instead reset to defaults rather than something nonsensical.  The checksum literally exists just for that "I re-orderd the effects or changed the pot meanings of the pots, and it should reset to something sane instead of becoming something senseless".  So let's make it better for that.  [ Also change the default for the pitch effect to be one octave up,   since that's the silly setting it was "designed" for ]  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Add USB host/device mode build options  This adds the option for the USB-C connector to be used as a way to communicate the UI state between two pedals over USB HID.  The default setting is that the pedal is a USB device that exposes both USB audio interfaces and a USB HID interface.  The other configuration is to build the "UI pedal" as a USB host: no audio capabilities, but it can communicate over the USB HID interface with the audio pedal, and it has the screen and the controls on it.  It also means that when you connect the audio box to a computer, not only do you get the audio interface, the new USB HID interface could be used to change all the effect settings dynamically from the computer too.  It's currently a specialized magic HID interface that is very closely tied to the particular effects versions on the pedal, so it's not very convenient as a control interface, but that can hopefully be fixed eventually with a slightly more thought out interface.  There could be variations on this model, where the audio box has possibly a single on-off stomp switch and maybe a master volume knob, so it doesn't have to be entirely hardcoded.  But since the audio pedal does have the EEPROM with effect settings, it would be entirely useful on its own even without the UI connected.  The UI pedal could also possibly talk MIDI, and thus extend on the UI that way.  This is all very hand-wavy and experimental.  I don't have such hardware yet, but I can test this by just connecting two of the existing pedals, with one acting as the audio pedal and the other as the UI pedal.  It is unclear if any actual user would want to do it this way, although Ricky Sheaves did point me at pedals like the Orange OMEC Teleport that he has.  That works as a limited version of my envisioned audio pedal - just without the built-in effects.  I'm doing this because I want to play with form factors once more, and separating the audio side from the UI means that I can play with one without having to worry about the other.  This is kind of a higher-level version of what I did with the codec and rp2354 boards for hardware layout.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Tremolo: fix the harmonic tremolo level drop  The old HARM formula was:      lo*(1 + k*lfo) + hi*(1 - k*lfo)  ==  (lo+hi) + k*lfo*(lo-hi)  The two filters (LP at 144.7 Hz, HP at 636.6 Hz) are not a complementary crossover pair, so `lo+hi` has a broad mid-frequency dip around 8 dB at 300 Hz. That made HARM noticeably quieter than NORM at the same gain staging.  New formula:      in + k*lfo*(lo - hi)  The modulation term `k*lfo*(lo-hi)` is identical; only the carrier changes from `lo+hi` to `in`.  - Unity gain at zero depth, matching NORM behaviour. - At mid frequencies the apparent depth per unit `k` is reduced. Increasing the depth control compensates. - At frequency extremes one branch dominates and depth is unchanged.  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Add tremolo effect with NORM and HARM modes  Just three controls.  RATE: 0.1-10 Hz, cubic DEPTH MODE (NORM/HARM).  NORM mode uses bipolar AM: gain = 1 + k*lfo, where k = depth/(2-depth). Average level stays at 1.0 at all depth settings, so 100% depth swings 0..2x rather than cutting average level by up to 6 dB.  HARM mode models the Fender 6G4 harmonic vibrato circuit with two one-pole filters: a LP at 144.7 Hz (220k/5nF) for the low branch and a HP at 636.6 Hz (1M/250pF, computed as in-LP) for the high branch. The LFO modulates them in opposite phase. The two corners are not complementary, so there is a broad mid-frequency dip and phasey recombination on summing, which is what gives the brownface character.  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Reduce reverb CPU load; minor echo optimisations  While testing, I discovered that loading reverb and echo at the same time resulted in audio artefacts. I don't have a profiler or cycle counter on the hardware, so I made these changes a couple at a time until the noise/distortion/crackle disappeared from the combined echo loop + reverb tail. Not very scientific, and my math may not be close to right, but it worked.  Reverb: - Drop from 12 to 10 parallel FBCFs; scale `REVERB_FIXEDGAIN` up from   0.007 to 0.0084 to preserve wet level with fewer combs; reverb still   sounds OK - Remove fractional-delay interpolation from the comb read: one buffer   load per comb instead of two, dropping the lerp multiply-adds - Eliminate the redundant `depth` clamp in the comb loop -- all ten   delay values (1215-1907) leave more than `REVERB_MOD_DEPTH` (6)   samples of headroom, so the branch was always taken; inline the   constant directly - Remove `reverb_flush` from the allpass chain; the 0.5 feedback   coefficient guarantees decay, so subnormals cannot accumulate there  Echo: - Precompute `tanhf(preamp_asymmetry)` once in `echo_init` as   `preamp_dc_offset`; the value is constant but `tanhf` is not   folded by the compiler from a `const` struct field - Cache equal-power blend gains (`dry_gain`, `wet_gain`); recompute   `fastsincos` only when `blend` drifts more than 0.001, matching the   existing `last_tone` guard pattern for the playback LPF  Rough cycles/sample saved (M33 @ 172.8 MHz, 3600 cycles/sample budget):  ``` | Change                                               | ~cycles/sample | |------------------------------------------------------|----------------| | 12 -> 10 combs (2 full comb iterations eliminated)   |             60 | | Remove lerp from comb read (2 loads -> 1)            |             70 | | Remove redundant `depth` clamp in comb loop          |             35 | | Remove `reverb_flush` from 6 allpasses               |             18 | | Precompute `tanhf(preamp_asymmetry)` in `echo_init`  |             50 | | Cache blend `fastsincos` (saved on ~99.9% of samples)|             12 | | **Total**                                            |       **~245** | ```  I say "rough" becuase is really just an instruction count and that't it. But, ~7% of the per-sample budget. Lerp removal and comb count reduction are the bulk of it. The `tanhf` saving is disproportionate for one line: it goes through `exp` internally (~50 cycles on M33). Comb buffer reads are non-sequential loads, so real savings may be somewhat less than the instruction count suggests.  NOTE: if we enable flush-to-zero by default on the MP33 FPU, we could save up to ~40 cycles/sample in addition to the stuff above. Might be as simple as    // FPU context is per-core; must be set on core 1 separately.   __set_FPSCR(__get_FPSCR() | 0x01000000); // FZ bit (bit 24)  at the top of `audio_processing()`. I'll leave that for Linus to suss out, though.  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Reverb: expand to 12 combs/6 allpasses, add per-comb LFO modulation  Standard Freeverb produces metallic ringing in long tails because fixed integer delays create sharp resonant peaks. Extending the filter bank and adding LFO modulation on each comb read pointer breaks up the periodicity.  DSP changes: - Comb count 8 -> 12: four additional delay lengths continuing the   original spacing pattern (1831, 1907, 1979, 2045 samples), all   within the existing `REVERB_COMB_SIZE = 2048` buffer - Allpass count 4 -> 6: two additional delays (153, 87 samples)   continuing the descending sequence - Four quadrature-phasor LFOs modulate each comb's read pointer:   complex-multiply rotation per sample, no `sincos` in the hot path;   rates 0.21/0.31/0.46/0.67 Hz (~3:2 geometric spacing to prevent   beating); phases staggered 0/0.25/0.5/0.75 cycles at init - Comb read upgraded from integer to linearly-interpolated fractional   delay; modulation depth clamped to `min(6 samples, buffer headroom)`   so the read pointer can never lap the write pointer - LFOs assigned round-robin to the 12 combs (`i % 4`)  Gain constants retuned for the larger filter bank: - `fixedgain` 0.015 -> 0.010 (proportional scaling for 12 combs) - `scalewet` 3.0 -> 1.5, `scaledry` 2.0 -> 1.2 (unity dry at 0% wet) - Damp range [0.0, 0.4] -> [0.1, 0.5]: fully undamped tails are   rarely useful and the old low end was dead space on the pot - Default Mix -50 -> -65 (0.175 wet), Damp 0 -> 15 (pole = 0.33)  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Add Freeverb reverb effect (Schroeder-Moorer, mono 48 kHz)  Jezar's public-domain Freeverb algorithm, ported to the pedal's sample-at-a-time mono path at 48 kHz.  DSP topology: - 8 parallel feedback comb filters (FBCF), all fed directly from   the input; each has a one-pole LP in its feedback path - 4 series Schroeder allpass filters on the summed comb output - Delay lengths are the canonical Freeverb 44100 Hz values scaled   to 48000 Hz (multiply by 48/44.1)  Parameters: - Mix: linear dry/wet, with `fixedgain` (0.015) on the comb input   and `scalewet`/`scaledry` (3.0/2.0) normalising levels - Room: feedback gain `g` in [0.70, 0.98] via roomscale/roomoffset - Damp: one-pole LP pole in [0, 0.4]; higher = more HF rolloff in   the FBCF feedback path  Two hardware workarounds required: - `reverb_flush()` manually zeros subnormals in the comb and allpass   buffers; the Cortex-M33 FPU does not flush-to-zero by default,   causing ~100x slowdown once the reverb tail decays below 1e-38 - All `reverb_state` fields including `.delay` are set in   `reverb_init()` because pico-sdk silently zeroes large static  objects during the .data copy from flash  Registered in `effects[]` between echo and pitch.  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Add preamp and vibrato effects  **Preamp** (`preamp.h`)  Wait, don't we already have a Boost effect? Yes, but ...  The current boost effect does wavefolding: it hard-clips by reflecting the signal back on itself, generating mostly odd-order harmonics with a sharp transition at the clip boundary. That's perfect for aggressive clipping or distortion pedal simulation, but it is not how a class-A analog front end behaves.  Preamp uses asymmetrically biased tanh saturation. Biasing the waveshaper off-centre generates even-order harmonics (mostly 2nd), which is the magick behind the warm character of class-A tube and JFET stages. The distortion onset is gradual; there is no clip boundary; just a soft knee. So, at moderate drive settings the signal is more coloured than clipped. Players who want 'always-on' front-end character rather than an obvious clipping stage tend to prefer this.  Usage: select Voice (Tube or JFET), dial Sat from 0.5x (clean) to 4x (hard clip), trim Level +/-20 dB. Works best early in the chain, typically first.  - Tube voice models two cascaded 12AX7 triode stages using `tanhf()` as the waveshaper. A fixed 0.15 grid-bias offset on each stage pushes the operating point off-centre, generating even-order harmonics for vintage-amp character. - An interstage DC block (~38 Hz, one-pole IIR) strips the stage-1 DC offset before stage 2 so the asymmetry doesn't accumulate. - JFET voice models a single common-emitter 2N5457-like stage with three frequency-domain features: an emitter-bypass low shelf (~120 Hz, -6 dB), an asymmetric `tanhf()` waveshaper with a 0.12 bias offset, and a Miller-cap HF rolloff (~9 kHz one-pole LPF). - Output normalization constants (`PREAMP_TUBE_NORM`, `PREAMP_JFET_NORM`) are precomputed at the default drive of 1.2x so unity gain is preserved (well, just barely above, actually) at the default settings.  **Vibrato** (`vibrato.h`)  Usage: set Rate (0.1-8 Hz) for LFO speed, Depth (0-5 ms) for pitch swing, Mix for dry/wet balance. At 100% wet you get pure pitch vibrato; blend in dry signal for chorus. 100% dry with a Rate of ~5 Hz makes for a nice rotary speaker emulation.  - Writes incoming samples into a 1024-entry ring buffer (~21 ms at 48 kHz) and reads back with a fractionally interpolated index offset by a sine LFO riding on a 6 ms center delay. - The center delay keeps the read head from overtaking the write head even at maximum depth (6 ms + 5 ms = 11 ms, well inside the 21 ms buffer). - Mix uses an equal-power crossfade: `dry = cos(0.25 * mix)`, `wet = sin(0.25 * mix)`, computed once in `vibrato_init` via `fastsincos`.  **effect.h**  - Add `desc_s()` unit descriptor (seconds) alongside the existing Hz/ms/dB helpers (will be used by a future reverb effect). - Insert `#include "preamp.h"` and `EFF(preamp)` immediately after `gate` (new index 1). - Insert `#include "vibrato.h"` and `EFF(vibrato)` immediately after `flanger` (new index 6). - **Note:** inserting effects mid-array shifts all subsequent effect indices, which shifts their EEPROM page addresses. You'll need to hold both encoders down with no USB connection to reset after first boot.  Signed-off-by: Ricky Sheaves <ricky@clevelandmusicco.com>

Add a workaround for invalid logbook begin pointers  Unfortunately there are several devices where an invalid logbook begin pointer occurs relative frequently. Typical examples are the Oceanic VT 4.1 and the Sherwood Wisdom 2. In such cases, the strict validation of the pointer causes the download to fail, without being able to download any dives at all.  Since the begin pointer is only needed to detect the oldest logbook entry, we can fall back to downloading the entire logbook ringbuffer. If we're lucky (and we usually are), we can detect the oldest entry by inspecting the logbook entries once they are downloaded (e.g. presence of uninitialized entries) and then the download will finish succesfully. In the worst case scenario, we'll be able to download at least some dives before hitting another error.

Let the ringbuffer function handle a full ringbuffer  The ringbuffer_distance() function has a parameter to specify whether a ringbuffer with identical begin/end pointers should be considered an empty or a full ringbuffer. Hence there is no need to handle the case of a full ringbuffer manually.

Suppress the warning if no O2 sensors are present  The warning about disabling the O2 sensors due to factory default calibration values, applies only if there is at least one calibrated O2 sensor present.  This has no effect on the calibration bits, because those are already zero if there are no calibrated O2 sensors present.

Integrate the connect step into the open function  There is no need to expose the two step connection setup of the underlying socket interface in the public api. Doing so may complicate the implementation on platforms where the native api is not based on the socket interface (e.g. Mac OS X).  Note that the function to connect based on the IrDA service name is removed. It's not used anywhere in libdivecomputer and since IrDA is an outdated technology nowadays, it's unlikely we'll need it in the future.

zlib: slide_hash: add MSAN annotation to suppress known read from uninitialised memory  slide_hash knowingly reads (possibly) uninitialised memory, see comment lower down about prev[n] potentially being garbage. In this case, the result is never used - so we don't care about MSAN complaining about this read.  By adding the no_sanitize("memory") attribute, clients of zlib won't see this (unnecessary) error when building and running with MemorySanitizer. An alternative approach is for clients to build zlib with -fsanitize-ignorelist=... where the ignorelist contains something like 'fun:slide_hash'. But that's more work and needs to be redone for any and all CI systems running a given project with MSAN. Adding this annotation to zlib's sources is overall more convenient - but also won't affect non-MSAN builds.  This specific issue was found while running git's test suite, but has also been reported by other clients, see e.g. #518.

media: rc: igorplugusb: fix control request setup packet  Commit eac69475b01f ("media: rc: igorplugusb: heed coherency rules") changed the control request storage from an embedded struct to an allocated pointer so it can obey DMA coherency rules.  However, the driver still passes &ir->request to usb_fill_control_urb(). That points the URB setup packet at the pointer field itself rather than at the allocated struct usb_ctrlrequest. Revert "x86/fpu: Refine and simplify the magic number check during signal return"  This reverts    dc8aa31a7ac2 ("x86/fpu: Refine and simplify the magic number check during signal return").  The aforementioned commit broke applications that construct signal frames in userspace (such as CRIU and gVisor) if the frame's xstate size is smaller than the kernel's fpstate->user_size.  Furthermore, this introduces a critical issue for checkpoint/restore tools like CRIU. If a process is checkpointed while inside a signal handler, its stack contains a signal frame formatted according to the source host's xstate capabilities.  If that process is later restored on a destination host with larger xstate capabilities (e.g., a newer CPU with more features enabled, resulting in a larger fpstate->user_size), the kernel will look for FP_XSTATE_MAGIC2 at the destination host's larger user_size offset instead of the offset encoded in the frame's fx_sw->xstate_size.  This causes the magic2 check to fail, forcing sigreturn to silently fall back to "FX-only" mode. Upon return from the signal handler, the process's extended state is reset to initial values instead of being restored, leading to silent data corruption.  The aforementioned commit cited    d877550eaf2d ("x86/fpu: Stop relying on userspace for info to fault in xsave buffer")  as justification to stop relying on userspace for the magic number check.  However, these two changes are fundamentally different. The last one only changed how much memory the kernel ensures is paged-in before running XRSTOR to prevent an infinite loop. It did not change the signal frame format or how the layout is validated.  Reverting this change restores the use of fx_sw->xstate_size for locating magic2 and restores the necessary sanity checks, ensuring that the signal frame remains self-describing and portable. drm/gem: fix race between change_handle and handle_delete  drm_gem_change_handle_ioctl leaves the old handle live in the IDR during the window between spin_unlock(table_lock) and the final spin_lock(table_lock). A concurrent drm_gem_handle_delete on the old handle succeeds in this window, decrements handle_count to 0, and frees the GEM object while the new handle's IDR entry still references it.  NULL the old handle's IDR entry before dropping table_lock so that any concurrent GEM_CLOSE on the old handle sees NULL and returns -EINVAL. Restore the old entry on the prime-bookkeeping error path. Revert "ipv6: preserve insertion order for same-scope addresses"  Chris Adams reported that preserving insertion order for same-scope addresses is causing SSH connections to be dropped after stopping a VM while running NetworkManager.  NetworkManager caches the IPv6 address configuration, when a RA arrives, it determines the list of addresses to configure and checks if the addresses are already in the right order in the kernel. If they aren't, NetworkManager removes and re-adds them to achieve the desired order.  As the order changes, NetworkManager is confused and reconfigures the addresses on every update. In addition, this would also affect to cloud tooling that relies on IPv6 addresses order to identify primary and secondaries addresses.  This reverts commit cb3de96eea66f5e4a580086c6a1be46e765f97f4.  Fixes: cb3de96eea66 ("ipv6: preserve insertion order for same-scope addresses") Reported-by: Chris Adams <linux@cmadams.net> Closes: https://lore.kernel.org/netdev/20260521135310.GC977@cmadams.net/ Signed-off-by: Fernando Fernandez Mancera <fmancera@suse.de> Link: https://patch.msgid.link/20260529112357.5079-1-fmancera@suse.de Signed-off-by: Jakub Kicinski <kuba@kernel.org>

Fix the dc sensor index fixup  fixup_dc_sample_sensors() would make sure that any pressure sensor indexes were in range of the cylinders by just clearing the pressure data if the sensor index was larger than the number of cylinders in the dive.  That certainly makes the sensor index data consistent, but at the cost of just dropping the sensor data entirely.  Dirk had some cases of odd sensor data (probably because of an older version of subsurface, but possibly due to removing cylinders manually or because of oddities with the downloader for the Atomic Aquatics Cobalt dive computer he used), and when re-saving the dive, the pressure data would magically just get removed due to this.  So rewrite the sensor data fixup to strive very hard to avoid throwing pressure sensor data away.  We do this by:   (a) generating a mask of sensor numbers seen   (b) checking if that mask is a subset of the cylinders we have, in      which case everything is fine.   (c) if it's not a subset, "compress" the sensor indexes to the minimal      range (ie if you had sensor indexes 3 and 6, rename 3 to 0, and 6      to 1).   (d) if it now fits in the cylinder mask we have, everything is fine   (e) if we still have more sensors than we have cylinders, leave the      data alone, but complain about it with SSRF_INFO() so that the user      is notified.  That final (e) case might be for dive computers that allow reporting pressure data for your buddy's cylinder too.  So it's odd, but not entirely crazy, and we now will keep the data.  You may have to add a fake cylinder to your dive to make it all make sense and avoid the informational warning.  This whole "we clear the pressure data" was at least partly hidden by two things:   (1) in the git save format, we don't rewrite dives unless you've      changed the dive some way, so old dives stay around with old data      in the save until explicitly changed.   (2) if you had multiple dive computers, and one dive computer does not      have any pressure data but another one does, our profile will use      that "other" dive computer pressure data (because often times you      might have only one dive computer that is air integrated, but you      still want to see the tank pressure when you look at other dive      computers - or you have one dive computer give pressure data for      your deco bottle, and another for your travel gas etc).  So those two facts hid the reality that we had actually cleared the tank sensor data for Dirk's dive with the Atomic Aquatics dive computer, because we'd still see pressure data in the profile, and the git data would still be the old one.  Until Dirk renumbered his dives, and the data was rewritten.  Signed-off-by: Linus Torvalds <torvalds@linux-foundation.org>

Improve on the timing logic a bit more  Time the warmup run to make a better estimate of how long to run the real runs.  We want to balance getting timely results with still actually having the time to actually traverse the full list a few times. Because five is obviously a holy random number, and is also how many times we run the test to try to de-noise the final number. Improve on map re-allocation strategy  Don't bother reallocating hugepage mappings, the cache associativity issues are hopefully not all that noticeable with big pages to begin with, and with fewer big pages to go around it's likely less effective to try to change the mapping anyway.  For the regular page case, force any remapping to over-map the old mapping, which will free the old pages.  That might cause the new mapping to have similar allocation patterns as the old one, but not using excessive amounts of memory still makes this the better option.
